ev.mng_m_first_saddle.text: They put you on a horse before you could properly walk. Your feet do not reach the stirrups, so they are tied on with a strap, and the old gelding plods along while you shout for joy across the whole steppe.
ev.mng_m_lambs.text: You have been trusted with the lambs. All day you sit on a knoll with a switch and count them on your fingers, and in the evening you drive them home - all present except one stubborn little thing you have to carry in your arms.
ev.mng_m_argal.text: In the morning you wander the pasture with a basket on your back and a wooden fork, gathering argal - dried dung for the hearth. There is no wood on the steppe, and the warmth of the yurt is your basket.
ev.mng_m_shagai.text: On a winter evening the children play shagai with sheep's anklebones. Roll a "horse" and your racer leaps ahead, roll a "camel" and it stands still. You win a whole handful of bones and fall asleep clutching them.
ev.mng_m_toono.text: Lying on the felt, you look up through the toono, the round smoke hole in the roof of the yurt. Through the hearth smoke you can see stars, and grandmother points: there are the Seven Old Men, and there the Golden Stake to which the Sky has tethered all the horses.
ev.mng_m_mares.text: In summer the mares are milked five or six times a day. You hold the foal against its dam so the milk will come, then take your turn churning kumis in the leather sack by the door - a thousand strokes, the elders say, no fewer.
ev.mng_m_white_month.text: The White Month - the new year. At dawn, in a new deel, you go round the yurts of your kin and bow to your elders, holding your hands beneath their elbows. Everywhere there is boiled mutton, white cream and milk spirit, and the old folk count how many springs you have seen.
ev.mng_m_child_jockey.text: At the races the riders are children - it is lighter for the horse. They put you bareback on a two-year-old, and for thirty versts you fly across the steppe singing the song that keeps a horse from tiring. You do not come first, but the horse is sound, and so are you.
ev.mng_m_wolf_cub.text: In a gully you find a den with three blind wolf cubs in it. The grown-ups decide: leave the she-wolf be, leave the cubs too - the Sky will judge. All night you lie awake listening to something howl far beyond the hill.
ev.mng_m_ovoo_stone.text: On the pass stands an ovoo - a cairn with a pole and blue ribbons. You walk round it three times sunwise, add your own pebble and flick milk to the four directions, as you were taught. Now the road will be easy.
ev.mng_m_threshold.text: Running in, you step right on the threshold of the yurt - and everyone freezes. The threshold is the neck of the house and must never be trodden on; in the khan's camp, they say, people have been put to death for it. Grandmother murmurs a charm over you and sprinkles milk on the sill.
ev.mng_m_five_arrows.text: The old storyteller tells of the foremother Alan Gho'a: she gave each of her five sons an arrow and each broke his, then she bound five together and none of them could. For a long time you turn twigs in your hands, trying to break the bundle.
ev.mng_m_move_camel.text: Moving camp. The yurt came down in a single morning: lattice walls, roof poles, felt and chests onto camels and into ox-drawn wagons. They sat you between the humps, and all day you sway above the steppe as if in a cradle.
ev.mng_m_spring_lambs.text: In spring the nights are still freezing, so the weak lambs are brought right into the yurt. You sleep with your arms round a warm, wet-nosed lamb, and towards morning it nuzzles your ear looking for milk.
ev.mng_m_first_haircut.text: Your hair, untouched since birth, has been cut for the first time. The guests take turns snipping a lock with shears tied with a blue ribbon, and each promises a gift - a lamb, a foal, a knife.
ev.mng_m_marmots.text: You are learning to hunt marmots: you wave a white tail and dance about, and the curious creature peeks out of its burrow. That is when you loose the arrow. The first marmot is yours, and its fat cures frostbite.
ev.mng_m_branding.text: In autumn the foals are branded. You hold the lasso pole while grandfather presses the red-hot tamga - your clan's mark. The foal squeals, you barely keep your feet, but the mark sits straight.
ev.mng_m_felt_making.text: In autumn the whole camp makes felt together. The wool is beaten with rods, soaked, spread on an old felt, rolled up and dragged across the steppe by a horse - and then everyone drinks kumis and sings while the felt dries.
ev.mng_m_summer_camp.text: Summer camp by the river is the best time of year. The grass reaches the stirrup, the mares give so much milk that people drink it instead of water, and in the evenings the young ones race to the ford and back.
ev.mng_m_winter_camp.text: The winter camp lies in a hollow out of the wind. The yurt walls are wrapped in double felt, and by the door there is a pen of dung and stones. Outside it has been blowing for three days, and you sit by the hearth listening to the blizzard howl in the smoke hole.
ev.mng_m_milk_sky.text: The first mare's milk of the year is not drunk: it is flung with a nine-hollowed spoon to the Sky, the Earth and the four directions. You hold the pail while the eldest whispers a blessing, and the drops glitter on the grass.
ev.mng_m_bard.text: A blind storyteller has come by. To a two-stringed khuur he sings till midnight of a hero whose horse understood speech and ran faster than thought. The yurt is packed full, and nobody stirs.
ev.mng_m_chinese_pot.text: Traders from the south have come to the camp. For two sheep they give an iron cauldron, for a fox skin a sack of millet, for a felt a length of silk. You bargain in gestures and, it seems, come out ahead.
ev.mng_m_caravan.text: A caravan files past the camp - a hundred camels with bales, bells, men in turbans and felt caps. They are travelling from Khwarazm to China, and one merchant gives you a handful of raisins such as you have never tasted.
ev.mng_m_silver_tree.text: In the khan's palace you see the silver tree made by a captive craftsman from Paris. Mare's milk flows from the mouths of silver lions at its roots, and wine, mead and rice beer from serpents twined round the trunk. At the top an angel blows a trumpet.
ev.mng_m_two_quarters.text: Karakorum has two quarters: one of Muslim merchants and the bazaar, the other of Chinese craftsmen. Between them stand Buddhist shrines, two mosques and a Nestorian church. In one day you hear five languages and the prayers of three faiths.
ev.mng_m_stone_turtle.text: By the gates of Karakorum lies a huge stone turtle - once it carried a slab with the khan's decree on its back. Children clamber over it and argue whether it really crawls to the river to drink at night.
ev.mng_m_paper_money.text: In Khanbaliq people pay with paper - sheets of mulberry bark stamped with the khan's seal. Refusing it is punishable by death. You turn the light grey sheet over in your hands and cannot believe someone will give you a sheep for it.
ev.mng_m_canal_barges.text: At the Jishuitan wharf stands a forest of masts: barges of rice from the distant Yangtze have come by the new canal right into the city. Porters sing, monks haggle over incense, and you count the boats and lose track in the second hundred.
ev.mng_m_observatory.text: On the observatory tower one of Guo Shoujing's astronomers shows you the bronze rings of the armillary sphere. With them, he says, they reckon a year of three hundred and sixty-five days and almost a quarter more - more precisely than anywhere under Heaven.
ev.mng_m_shangdu.text: In spring the court leaves Khanbaliq for the summer capital, Shangdu - out to the steppe and the cool air. Carts, the elephants carrying the khan's palanquin, herds and flocks stretch for tens of versts, and it seems to you that the whole world is on the move with you.
ev.mng_m_sarai_bazaar.text: The bazaar of Sarai hums in every language: Russians sell sable and honey, Genoese from Caffa sell cloth, Khwarazmians raisins, and by the wall sit slaves with shackles on their feet. You squeeze your way to a stall of sweet halva.
ev.mng_m_volga_ice.text: In winter the Volga freezes and whole trains cross on the ice - wagons, camels, troops of horsemen. You slide across on a sled of cowhide and listen to the ice boom and crack under the hooves.
ev.mng_m_azan.text: Over the clay roofs of Sarai the muezzin calls from the minaret. Not long ago people here prayed to the Sky; now Khan Özbeg has ordered mosques built, and one by one the neighbours are learning to read Arabic words.
ev.mng_m_tiles.text: Persian masters are laying turquoise tiles on the dome of a new mosque. You stand below, head tipped back, and cannot tell where the dome ends and the sky begins.
ev.mng_m_ujan.text: In summer the Ilkhan's nobles leave hot Tabriz for the pastures of Ujan. The city is left to the Persians, and the Mongols are back in their tents with kumis and herds, and the old men say: "Now this is life - not walls."
ev.mng_m_poets.text: At a nobleman's feast Persian verses are recited - of wine, nightingales and the frailty of kingdoms. The Mongol noyan beside you understands not a word, yet claps loudly in all the right places.
ev.mng_m_grandkids_tales.text: Grandchildren - your own and the neighbours' - sit round you, and you tell them what the steppe was like when you were young: what blizzards, what horses, what people. They believe half of it, and quite right too.
ev.mng_m_dowry_yurt.text: A bride brings her own yurt to her husband's camp: the lattice, the felt and the dowry chest follow behind on a wagon. As you watch the new white yurt go up beside the others, the camp grows a little bigger.
ev.mng_m_aaruul.text: On the roof of the yurt slices of curd - aaruul - dry on a felt. You pinch them one at a time when nobody is looking and suck them, sour and hard as pebbles.
ev.mng_m_dust_storm.text: A spring storm has blown in from the Gobi: the sky turned yellow, sand lashes your face, and the whole camp had to hold the yurt down by its ropes. By evening it is over, and you spend a long time shaking sand out of the felt, the cauldrons and your hair.
ev.mng_m_horse_name.text: At last you have a horse of your own - a dun with a little white star. You take a long time choosing its name and whisper it into its ear, as the old men teach, so the horse knows who its master is.
ev.mng_m_archery_boys.text: The children shoot little bows at a sack stuffed with wool. Miss, miss, miss - and suddenly an arrow quivers right in the middle. The old man teaching you nods: "The Sky saw that."
ev.mng_m_khadag.text: An honoured guest has entered the yurt. You offer him a bowl of kumis with both hands, as is proper, and sit in your place - left of the door, where the young belong. The guest is pleased: in this yurt they know how things are done.
ev.mng_m_night_guard.text: At night you guard the horse herd. Wind, stars, horses snorting, and somewhere beyond the hill a wolf howling. You hold your bow across your knees and hum to yourself till dawn to keep awake.
ev.mng_m_sheep_count.text: In the evening the flock comes back to the yurt, and you stand by the pen watching the sheep stream past like a grey river. You must not count them aloud - it brings the evil eye - so you count silently and smile: there are more.
ev.mng_m_foreign_envoys.text: Envoys from the distant land of the Franks have ridden through the camp - in grey robes, barefoot even in the frost. People laugh at them, but feed them: such is the khan's law - an envoy must not be harmed.
ev.mng_m_throat_song.text: By the fire a herdsman sings a long song, an urtyn duu. One note is held so long it seems the steppe itself is singing, not a man. You join the refrain and do not notice the embers dying.
ev.mng_m_boiled_lamb.text: A sheep has been slaughtered. Nothing is wasted: meat for the cauldron, guts for sausage, bones for the children's shagai, the skin for a deel. As the guest of honour you are handed the fat tail - the choicest piece.
ev.mng_m_lost_in_fog.text: In the fog you lose the camp. No hill, no star. You let the reins go slack - the horse knows the way - and two hours later it brings you right to your own yurt, snorting crossly.
ev.mng_m_tamga_seal.text: For the first time you watch a scribe write in Uyghur letters - from top to bottom, as if drawing a knotted cord down the page. He writes out your name, and you stare a long time at that little black snake: it is you.
ev.mng_m_khutulun_wrestle.text: At the festival a girl challenges the young men to wrestle - as Khutulun, Khaidu's daughter, is said to have done; she would marry no man who could not throw her. You watch breathlessly as she throws her third in a row.
ev.mng_m_kumis_hangover.text: At yesterday's feast you drank more kumis than you should, and arkhi - strong milk spirit - besides. In the morning your head booms like a shaman's drum, and the elders laugh: "Then the feast was a success."
ev.mng_m_eagle.text: High above you a golden eagle wheels. An old falconer says a bird like that can take a fox, even a young wolf - and he goes still, as if working out how he might catch it.
ev.mng_m_nomad_school.text: Children have been gathered in a yurt at the camp: a scribe teaches the Uyghur letters on a board strewn with sand. With your finger you draw your first letter, "a" - it looks like a horse rearing up.
ev.mng_m_mongol_china_bride.text: In Khanbaliq Mongol women still wear the tall boqta headdress with its plume, and Chinese women silk skirts and hairpins. You notice your Mongol friend secretly trying on hairpins - and your Chinese friend trying on a boqta.
